tagline.text: Seven Bukidnon tribes gather for rituals and street dancing

location.label: Location
location.text: Kaamulan Park and Capitol Grounds area, Malaybalay City, Bukidnon

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Varies by year (in 2026: March 19 to April 23; street dancing on April 18)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (local food and city transport per day; excludes flights, lodging and bus)

children.text: Kaamulan is Mindanao's signature cultural festival, where the seven indigenous tribes of Bukidnon gather in Malaybalay to showcase traditional rituals, dance and music. The pre-dawn rituals and the tribal parade are the highlights.

The Kaamulan Festival is an indigenous cultural festival held in Malaybalay, the capital of Bukidnon province in northern Mindanao. The name comes from "amul" in the Bukidnon language, Binukid, meaning "to gather." Originally it referred to a meeting where tribal elders discussed matters affecting the land and the people, and that gathering could be a datuship (chieftain installation) ritual, a wedding, a harvest thanksgiving, or a peace pact between tribes. Today the festival turns all of these into a month-long celebration. Unlike many other Philippine festivals such as Sinulog, it is not built around a patron saint's feast or a historical event; indigenous culture itself is the star.

Its roots go back to the 1970s. It is said to have begun on May 15, 1974, when a Malaybalay vice mayor invited indigenous people to dance at Plaza Rizal during the town fiesta. In 1977 it became the regional festival of Northern Mindanao (Region X), and that November 25–27 it was held for the first time as a full festival. The timing has changed several times since. From 1978 to 1998 it was held on the first Friday of September; from 1999 it ran from the second half of February to March 10, the province's founding anniversary; and in 2014 it moved to August for the province's 100th anniversary. In 2026 it was announced to open on March 19 and run through April 23. Because the timing changes so often, be sure to check the official schedule for the year you plan to visit.

The festival honors seven tribes: the Bukidnon, Higaonon, Talaandig, Manobo, Matigsalug, Tigwahanon and Umayamnon. The Talaandig live around Lantapan and Talakag and are known for embroidery and patchwork, the Matigsalug live along the Salug River, and the Tigwahanon along the Tigwa River. The Umayamnon are famous for their beadwork and brass jewelry. Each tribe has its own language, clothing and songs, so paying attention to the colors and ornaments of the costumes in the parade is enough to see the differences. One thing worth knowing: not every dance team on stage is made up of tribe members; many teams represent municipalities and cities and reinterpret tribal stories in dance.

For a traveler, the appeal of Kaamulan is that the audience's seat and the ritual's ground are close together. You can watch a ritual in the dark before dawn, with gongs, drums and the prayers of tribal elders right in front of you, and later that same morning watch street dancers in splendid costumes march past. The rituals and the parade are only part of it: over a month or more, an agricultural fair, a garden show, culture and arts exhibits, concerts and sports competitions run alongside. It is smaller than the big-city festivals, but that makes it easier to get close and to chat or haggle with locals. At the same time, rituals held in sacred places are solemn events, so ask permission before taking photos and follow the instructions of the staff.
This ritual opens the festival. In 2026 it was held on March 19 at

at the Kaamulan Capitol Grounds together with a ribbon cutting. Tribal elders offer prayers and announce the start of the festival. Because it takes place before sunrise, it is pleasantly cool, which makes it a good time to watch. That evening, an opening concert and a fireworks show were also held.

blocks.title: Parade of the seven tribes and street dancing competition

children.text: This is the festival's biggest event. In 2026, on April 18 at

, the parade set off from the Old Pine Hills Hotel (Sumpong, Sayre Highway) and marched to the Capitol Grounds, with street dancing, ground presentations and a float competition all taking place at once. Teams representing municipalities and cities pass one after another, and tribal costumes blend with the rhythm of drums and gongs. Earlier that day at
, the Pamalabag ha Pangampo ritual was held at the same place. You watch from the roadside while standing, so there is little cost, but it is the busiest day, so head out early.

blocks.title: Seven Tribes Tribal Mass Wedding (Kag Asawaha)

children.text: Couples from the tribal communities marry together in the traditional way. In 2026 it was held on April 8 at
at the Centennial Stage in Kaamulan Park. It is one of the few chances to see wedding attire and rites up close.

blocks.title: Traditional cooking show and agricultural fair

children.text: In 2026, a traditional indigenous cooking show was held at Kaamulan Park on April 9, while the Agri-Fair and the culture and arts exhibit ran at the Capitol Grounds from opening day through April 23. You can browse and buy traditional food, Bukidnon specialties and handicrafts, so there is plenty to enjoy even if you come on a day other than the street dancing.
In 2026, on April 17 at

, a stage show introducing Bukidnon culture was held at the Kaamulan Open Theater. It is a seated performance, and many guides say it helps you understand the background before watching the street dancing the next day.
In 2026 this ritual was held on April 17 at

at Calawaig Creek in Kaamulan Park. It has a strong flavor of purification and prayer by the water and is described as the spiritual close of the festival. You have to get up early, but this is the calmest setting in which to watch a ritual.

On opening night and on the night of April 19, concerts and a pyromusical fireworks show were held at the Capitol Grounds. Separately, agricultural events such as a national horse show and a fish show, motorcycle and bicycle races, golf, tennis and badminton tournaments, and sports events such as a marathon are held around the province. Many of these have little to do with culture, so it is more efficient to pick only the ones you care about from the schedule.

Get up and head to the Sumpong area. At this hour a dawn ritual begins at the Old Pine Hills Hotel, so go early if you want to watch from close. It is dark, so a flashlight and a warm layer are helpful.
The street dancing and tribal parade set off. The route follows Sayre Highway and Fortich Street to the Capitol Grounds. Claim a spot along the road before the sun gets high and take your photos.
After the parade, have a meal and rest at the market or the fair grounds at the Capitol Grounds. Midday is hot and dusty.
Browse the tribal handicrafts and local products at the agricultural fair and the culture exhibit.
If an evening show or concert is on, enjoy it at the Kaamulan Open Theater and the Capitol Grounds.

children.text: Take a bus from Cagayan de Oro to Malaybalay, arrive and drop your bags at your lodging. Look around the exhibits and the fair in Kaamulan Park.
Watch a cultural performance at the Open Theater and turn in early.
Watch the dawn ritual and the street dancing.
Visit nearby
Dahilayan
or sights in town, then head home.
Event dates change every year. Book flights and lodging soon after the official schedule is announced.
Flights operate from Manila (NAIA) to Laguindingan Airport (CGY) near Cagayan de Oro. Travel time and fares vary by airline and season, so check a booking site.
Malaybalay also has an airport, but it is hard for ordinary travelers to use, so most people fly into Cagayan de Oro.

items.title: By bus from Cagayan de Oro

children.text: Buses to Malaybalay run from the Agora Bus Terminal (Lapasan) in Cagayan de Oro. RTMI buses are said to leave about every
2 hours
The trip takes about
2–2.5 hours
, and an air-conditioned bus fare is described as roughly ₱250~400. Check the latest announcements for fares and times.
Since you need a shuttle or taxi from the airport to the terminal, it is safest to allow 4–5 hours in total from the airport to Malaybalay.
Driving from the airport along Sayre Highway is said to take about
2 hours
. A taxi or chartered car is reported at roughly ₱1,500 or more, but you will need to negotiate.
Checkpoints are set up during the festival. Bags may be inspected, so pack light.
Between central Malaybalay and the park you can take a motorela (three-wheeled taxi); short rides are said to cost about ₱10~15. Carry small bills.
On parade day the Fortich Street area is closed to traffic, so it is suggested that you park at the bus terminal or in the Casisang area and take a motorela in.

The timing of Kaamulan changes from year to year, so it is hard to pin down. Recently it has opened in late March and run to late April, with the highlight, the street dancing, held around the last weekend. In 2026 it was on April 18.

Schedules and venues, even the names of events and the order of the tribes, change every year, so be sure to check the Bukidnon provincial and Malaybalay city tourism announcements before you leave. This is a time of transition from the dry season to the rainy season, so it can be hot by day with sudden showers.

Central Malaybalay is the most convenient place to stay. Places often mentioned include Pine Hills Hotel around Fortich Street, Green Ridge Apartelle on Carbajal Street and Loft Hotel. They are close to the venues, but during parade week they fill up early and can be noisy. For a quieter stay, resorts in Casisang and Sumpong are a good choice, though you will need a motorela. If you cannot find a room, you can also stay in Valencia City, about
20km
to the south, and head out early on parade morning.

Look out for binaki, a Bukidnon corn snack, and local coffee. The agricultural fair sells local produce and traditional food. Prices for water and snacks can rise during the festival, so it is best to stock up at the market beforehand, and bring plenty of cash. Many small shops and stalls do not accept electronic payment.
On parade day you must go out early to get a spot along the road. Stay in Malaybalay the night before.
Mobile signal may drop or weaken briefly, so download offline maps and decide on a meeting point in advance.
Bring plenty of cash and small bills, and leave large bags at your lodging or the luggage storage at the Cagayan de Oro terminal.
It is dusty, so bring a mask or scarf, and you will need a hat and plenty of water during the day.
When photographing tribal elders or ritual scenes, ask permission first, and do not use flash or drones during sacred rituals.
The schedule changes every year, so check the latest announcements from Bukidnon province and Malaybalay city before you go.
Do not try to see every event in a single day; it is better to pick one or two, such as a dawn ritual, the parade or an evening show.
If you can, buy handicrafts directly from tribal communities to support them. Ask the price before buying and haggle politely.
On parade day roads are closed and there may be checkpoints and bag inspections, so check prohibited items and closed areas beforehand.
The parade day is extremely crowded, so watch out for pickpockets and lost items. Keep valuables in front of your body.
Drones are reported to be confiscated, so check first whether they are allowed.
Rituals are sacred events, so follow staff instructions and do not step into restricted areas.
Schedules and venues change every year and blogs disagree on dates, so give priority to official announcements.
Check the latest travel safety information for Mindanao before you leave.
The provincial capital where the festival is held; the town center and Kaamulan Park are close together.
A resort area on the Bukidnon highlands, good to combine with the festival. Check the travel time locally.
